question: The classic triad of Battered Baby Syndrome (Caffey syndrome) comprises:

answers.text: Subdural haematoma, retinal haemorrhage, and posterior rib/metaphyseal fractures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Caffey (1946) described this triad caused by repetitive shaking — rotational forces shear bridging veins (SDH), fundal vessels (retinal haemorrhage), and generate classic fracture patterns.

answers.text: Epidural haematoma, corneal abrasion, and diaphyseal femur fractures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Epidural haematomas are arterial bleeds from head impacts, not the shaking mechanism. Diaphyseal fractures are less specific for abuse than metaphyseal or posterior rib fractures.

answers.text: Subarachnoid haemorrhage, vitreous haemorrhage, and spiral forearm fractures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While subarachnoid and vitreous haemorrhage can occur in AHT, the classic Caffey triad specifically names subdural haematoma and retinal haemorrhage. Spiral fractures suggest twisting/pulling, not the classic triad.

answers.text: Contrecoup contusion, optic nerve damage, and transverse vertebral fractures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Contrecoup contusion is a different mechanism (blunt head impact). Optic nerve and transverse vertebral fractures are not part of the Caffey triad.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review BBS: the triad is subdural haematoma (not epidural), retinal haemorrhage (not corneal), and posterior rib/metaphyseal fractures (not diaphyseal). These injury patterns together are virtually pathognomonic for abusive head trauma.
Correct. The Caffey triad: subdural haematoma + retinal haemorrhage + metaphyseal/posterior rib fractures. All three arise from the shaking mechanism and are highly specific for abusive head trauma.
